title: 6.7 — Autocorrelation and the Durbin–Watson Test
breadcrumb: Unit VI → Regression and linear models → 6.7 Autocorrelation and Durbin–Watson
engineName: Understand serial correlation in regression disturbances, derive its consequences for OLS inference, and apply the Durbin–Watson diagnostic.
objectives: Define autocorrelation in regression disturbances and distinguish it from heteroscedasticity.
Explain how serial correlation affects OLS efficiency and conventional standard errors.
Recognize positive and negative serial correlation from residual patterns.
Calculate and interpret the Durbin–Watson statistic.
State the hypotheses, bounds and limitations of the Durbin–Watson test.
Identify when alternative tests or GLS-type corrections are needed.

prereq.name: Classical linear regression assumptions
prereq.why: The covariance matrix of the disturbance determines the OLS variance formula.

prereq.name: Residuals, fitted values and OLS
prereq.why: Durbin–Watson is computed from regression residuals.

prereq.name: Time-series lag notation and autocorrelation
prereq.why: Serial correlation concerns dependence across observations ordered in time.

traps: Autocorrelation is covariance across different observations; heteroscedasticity is non-constant variance within observations.
With exogeneity, serial correlation alone need not bias OLS coefficients, but OLS is generally inefficient and conventional standard errors are unreliable.
DW is approximately 2(1−r̂₁), where r̂₁ is the first-order sample residual autocorrelation.
DW values near 0 suggest positive first-order serial correlation; values near 2 suggest none; values near 4 suggest negative serial correlation.
The DW statistic lies between 0 and 4.
The usual DW bounds test has an inconclusive region; do not force a decision when d lies between dL and dU (or their upper-tail counterparts).
The standard DW test is not appropriate in its usual form when lagged dependent variables are included among regressors.
DW tests first-order serial correlation, not every possible higher-order dependence pattern.
Durbin's h or Breusch–Godfrey LM may be needed in dynamic models or for higher-order serial correlation.
Do not confuse a DW statistic with a p-value; formal decisions use bounds or an appropriate reference procedure.
howto: Order observations in time and fit the stated regression. Compute residuals eₜ, then DW=Σₜ₌₂ⁿ(eₜ−eₜ₋₁)²/Σₜ₌₁ⁿeₜ². Interpret the value on the 0–4 scale, but use the DW lower and upper critical bounds for a formal decision. State the inconclusive region and check whether lagged dependent variables invalidate the usual test. If the model is dynamic or a higher-order alternative is relevant, consider Durbin's h or Breusch–Godfrey.

sheet: Autocorrelation: Cov(uₜ,uₛ|X)≠0 for some t≠s; first-order AR(1): uₜ=ρuₜ₋₁+εₜ.
Homoscedasticity concerns Var(uₜ|X); autocorrelation concerns cross-time covariance.
Under exogeneity OLS may remain unbiased, but is generally inefficient and conventional SEs may be wrong.
DW range is 0 to 4; 0 indicates strong positive, 2 no first-order, 4 strong negative autocorrelation.
Positive autocorrelation: successive residuals tend to have same sign; negative: signs tend to alternate.
DW bounds: d<dL evidence positive; d>dU no evidence positive; between dL,dU inconclusive.
For negative autocorrelation use 4−d and the upper-tail bounds.
Usual DW assumptions exclude lagged dependent variable regressors; consider BG or Durbin h in dynamic models.
tricks: If DW is around 1, approximate r̂₁≈1−DW/2≈0.5.
If DW is around 3, approximate r̂₁≈−0.5.
A value between the critical bounds is inconclusive, not acceptance of H₀.
When yₜ₋₁ is a regressor, do not apply the ordinary DW bounds mechanically.
shortcuts: DW≈2(1−r̂₁) is a quick interpretation tool, not a replacement for the bounds test.
DW below 2 points toward positive first-order residual correlation; above 2 points toward negative correlation.
Always state whether the alternative is positive, negative or two-sided before applying DW bounds.
For a dynamic regression with a lagged dependent variable, use an appropriate alternative such as Breusch–Godfrey rather than the ordinary DW bounds.
remember: DW addresses first-order serial correlation in a regression setting; it is not a universal residual independence test.
Robust standard errors and GLS corrections address different objectives and assumptions.

scenes.title: Rebuild covariance across observations
scenes.objective: Distinguish variance within one observation from covariance across observations.
body: A regression disturbance uₜ is the part of yₜ not explained by the regressors. Its variance Var(uₜ|X) describes the spread of the error at time t.
Cov(uₜ,uₛ|X) describes whether errors at two different times move together. If this covariance is nonzero, the disturbances are correlated across observations.
Autocorrelation in time-series regression usually means this cross-time covariance depends on the lag between t and s. It is not the same assumption as constant variance.

items.recall: The conditional variance of the error at observation t.
refresh: It describes the spread of the error distribution at a particular time point, after conditioning on the regressors.
It is a within-observation quantity and does not tell us whether errors at two different times move together.
For example, Var(uₜ|X)=4 says the conditional variance at time t is four; it does not specify Cov(uₜ,uₜ₋₁|X).

items.recall: The conditional covariance between adjacent-time disturbances.
refresh: It measures whether the error at time t moves systematically with the error one period earlier.
A positive covariance indicates same-direction movement on average; a negative covariance indicates opposite-direction movement.
This cross-time covariance is the quantity involved in first-order autocorrelation.

items.recall: Dependence between disturbances one time period apart, commonly represented by Cov(uₜ,uₜ₋₁|X)≠0.
refresh: The word first-order refers to lag one: compare uₜ with uₜ₋₁.
It is a statement about dependence across observations, not about the marginal variance at each time point.
A common representation is the AR(1) disturbance equation uₜ=ρuₜ₋₁+εₜ.

ask.q: Which quantity directly describes serial dependence?
ask.nudge: It is a covariance between different time points.

scenes.title: Why residuals may run in sequences
scenes.objective: Recognize positive and negative serial dependence.
body: If a disturbance is positive this period, positive autocorrelation makes a positive disturbance next period more likely. Residuals tend to appear in runs of the same sign.
Negative autocorrelation produces alternation: a positive residual is more likely to be followed by a negative one, and vice versa.
A residual plot against time can reveal these patterns, but visual inspection is only a diagnostic.

scenario.teaser: Residuals remain positive for several consecutive periods
scenario.title: A run of same-sign residuals
body: Imagine residuals from a quarterly sales regression. Several consecutive residuals are positive, followed by several negative residuals.
Such runs suggest that the errors may be moving together over time rather than behaving independently.
This pattern can arise when a dynamic feature has been omitted or when the disturbance itself follows a time-series process.
The order of the observations matters: rearranging the residuals would destroy the time sequence and could hide the dependence.
A useful first diagnostic is therefore a residual-versus-time plot, followed by a lag-one residual plot or a formal test.
Persistent same-sign residuals often indicate that the regression has left a systematic time pattern unexplained.
scenario.q: Which direction of first-order autocorrelation is suggested by long same-sign runs?

ask.q: What residual sign pattern is typical of negative autocorrelation?

scenes.title: Visualise residual dependence
scenes.objective: Connect the lag-one relationship to serial correlation.
body: A lag plot places eₜ on one axis and eₜ₋₁ on the other. An upward association suggests positive first-order residual autocorrelation; a downward association suggests negative association.
A cloud with no clear linear trend is consistent with little first-order correlation, though absence of a visible pattern does not prove independence.
Always inspect residuals in their time order as well as through a lag plot.

viz.caption: A lag-one residual plot assesses whether eₜ tends to move with eₜ₋₁.

scenario.teaser: The lag-one residual plot slopes downward
scenario.title: Alternating residual movements
body: Suppose the lag plot of eₜ against eₜ₋₁ shows a clear downward trend.
Large positive residuals tend to follow negative residuals and vice versa. This is evidence consistent with negative first-order autocorrelation.
The formal DW statistic can summarise this first-order pattern, but its critical bounds must still be used for a test decision.

A lag plot is useful because the horizontal axis shows the previous residual and the vertical axis shows the current residual. The slope direction gives a visual clue about the sign of lag-one dependence.
A positive association does not establish the full disturbance model, and a weak association does not rule out higher-order serial correlation.
Use the plot alongside the model specification and a formal diagnostic rather than treating it as a stand-alone test.
scenario.q: Would the DW statistic tend to be below or above 2?
scenario.answer: Above 2, because the first-order residual autocorrelation is negative.

ask.q: What does an upward lag-one residual pattern suggest?
ask.nudge: Successive residuals tend to share their sign.

scenes.title: AR(1) disturbances and OLS consequences
scenes.objective: Model first-order serial correlation and state its consequences.

blocks.body: A common model is uₜ=ρuₜ₋₁+εₜ, with |ρ|<1 for covariance stationarity under the usual innovation assumptions. Positive ρ produces persistence; negative ρ produces alternation.

If the conditional mean is correctly specified and regressors are strictly exogenous, E(uₜ | X₁,…,Xₙ)=0, serial correlation alone need not bias OLS coefficients. However, OLS is generally inefficient relative to a correctly specified GLS estimator.
The usual OLS covariance formula assumes no cross-observation error covariance. Under serial correlation, conventional standard errors and the resulting t and F tests can be unreliable.

flow.caption: Separate mean assumptions from error covariance

nodes.label: OLS generally inefficient; usual SE unreliable

ask.q: Does autocorrelation alone necessarily bias OLS under exogeneity?
ask.nudge: Separate the conditional mean assumption from the covariance assumption.

scenes.title: Worked example: classify the disturbance process
scenes.problem: A regression disturbance follows uₜ=0.7uₜ₋₁+εₜ. What kind of serial dependence is represented?

steps.say: Read the coefficient on the lagged disturbance.
steps.why: The AR(1) coefficient controls the sign and strength of first-order persistence.
Positive shocks tend to be followed by shocks of the same sign.
Under standard innovation assumptions, this is compatible with a stationary AR(1) disturbance.
The correlation at lag one is positive and substantial.

ask.q: If ρ were −0.6, what would change?
ask.nudge: The sign indicates the direction of adjacent-time dependence.

scenes.title: Derive the Durbin–Watson statistic
scenes.objective: Understand what the DW ratio measures.

blocks.body: For OLS residuals e₁,…,eₙ ordered in time, DW=Σₜ₌₂ⁿ(eₜ−eₜ₋₁)² / Σₜ₌₁ⁿeₜ². The numerator measures squared changes between adjacent residuals; the denominator scales by total residual magnitude.

Expanding the numerator and using the endpoint approximation gives DW≈2(1−r̂₁), where r̂₁ is the sample lag-one residual autocorrelation. This makes DW near 0 a sign of positive correlation, near 2 a sign of little first-order correlation, and near 4 a sign of negative correlation.
The statistic is between 0 and 4. The approximation is useful for interpretation; formal testing uses critical bounds that depend on sample size, regressors and significance level.

ask.q: What approximate residual autocorrelation corresponds to DW=1.2?

steps.why: This is the denominator of the DW ratio.
A value below 2 suggests positive first-order serial correlation; formal inference requires critical bounds.

scenes.title: Formal DW bounds test
scenes.objective: State hypotheses and handle the inconclusive region.

blocks.body: For H₀:ρ=0 against H₁:ρ>0, compare d with lower and upper bounds dL and dU. If d<dL, reject H₀ in favour of positive autocorrelation. If d>dU, do not reject for positive autocorrelation. If dL≤d≤dU, the result is inconclusive.
For H₀:ρ=0 against H₁:ρ<0, use the transformed statistic 4−d and the corresponding DW bounds. Equivalently, values near 4 are evidence of negative serial correlation.

A two-sided decision combines the positive and negative tails, retaining inconclusive regions. The exact bounds depend on n, number of regressors (excluding the intercept) and the chosen significance level.

ask.q: What is the correct decision when dL<d<dU?
ask.nudge: The test does not give a definite rejection or non-rejection in this interval.

scenes.title: Worked example: interpret a bounds result
scenes.objective: Avoid forcing a decision in the inconclusive region.
scenes.problem: Suppose the tabulated bounds are dL=1.20 and dU=1.45, and the observed DW statistic is 1.32. What is the conclusion for the positive-autocorrelation test?

steps.say: Locate the observed statistic relative to the bounds.
steps.why: The observed value lies between the lower and upper critical bounds.
Neither rejection nor non-rejection is established by the bounds procedure.
Do not label this result as proof of no autocorrelation or as a rejection.

ask.q: Can we conclude that there is no positive autocorrelation?
ask.nudge: An inconclusive outcome is neither a rejection nor a non-rejection.

solution.say: Substitute 2.8: r̂₁≈1−1.4=−0.4, suggesting negative first-order residual autocorrelation.

scenes.title: Limitations and alternative tests
scenes.objective: Know when ordinary DW is not the right procedure.

blocks.body: The standard Durbin–Watson bounds test is not valid in its usual form when a lagged dependent variable appears among the regressors. The statistic may still be reported descriptively, but its usual critical bounds should not be used mechanically.
DW is designed for first-order serial correlation. A Breusch–Godfrey LM test can test higher-order alternatives and is suitable in many dynamic regression settings.

For certain models containing a lagged dependent variable, Durbin's h statistic provides an alternative test under its assumptions. If its variance expression is unsuitable, use an appropriate BG procedure.

ask.q: Which test is a common alternative for higher-order serial correlation?
ask.nudge: It is the LM test named after Breusch and Godfrey.

scenes.title: Exam traps: autocorrelation and DW
scenes.objective: Correct common statements about serial correlation.
scenes.intro: Mark each statement true or false.

items.claim: Autocorrelation concerns covariance between disturbances at different time points.
items.why: It is cross-observation dependence, unlike heteroscedasticity which concerns unequal conditional variances.
This approximation links the statistic to the first-order sample residual autocorrelation.

items.claim: A DW statistic near 4 suggests positive first-order autocorrelation.
items.why: Values near 4 suggest negative first-order autocorrelation.

items.claim: The DW bounds test has an inconclusive region.
items.why: Values between dL and dU do not yield a definite decision.

items.claim: The usual DW bounds can be applied without qualification when a lagged dependent variable is a regressor.
items.why: The standard DW test is not valid in its usual form in that dynamic-regression setting.

scenes.title: Summary: diagnose without overclaiming
scenes.objective: Consolidate the meaning and limitations of DW.
body: Autocorrelation is dependence between disturbances at different times. It differs from heteroscedasticity, which concerns non-constant conditional variance.
Under exogeneity, OLS coefficients may remain unbiased, but serial correlation generally reduces efficiency and invalidates conventional standard-error calculations.
DW=Σ(eₜ−eₜ₋₁)²/Σeₜ² and DW≈2(1−r̂₁). Its range is 0–4: near 0 positive, near 2 little first-order, near 4 negative correlation.
Use dL and dU bounds and report inconclusive outcomes honestly. For dynamic regressions or higher-order alternatives, consider Durbin's h or Breusch–Godfrey.

ask.q: What is the most important limitation to remember about the usual DW test?
ask.nudge: Think about lagged dependent variables and the order of serial correlation.
